newsitem.title: USA: Last week of holiday shopping crucial to retailers.
newsitem.headline: Last week of holiday shopping crucial to retailers.

text.p: Brisk sales have made the holidays cheery so far for many retailers, but these last eight days before Christmas are the most crucial for this year's shorter shopping season.
While many Americans may be hoping for a white Christmas, a blizzard in the weather forecast is the last thing retailers want to see, industry analysts said Tuesday.

"I think it's going to be a mad rush, and I think there is a fair amount of risk," said Dean Ramos, a retail analyst at brokerage Dain Bosworth Inc. "If the East Coast had 14 inches of snow this Saturday, it wouldn't be a good thing."

With five fewer shopping days between Thanksgiving and Christmas this year, stores must ring up about 15 percent more in sales each day just to match last year. Most retail analysts say stores are doing just that but need to keep up the pace.
"It's more intensified buying," said Howard Eilenberg, a retail analyst for LJR Redbook Research. His research firm expects a 5.5 percent increase in sales over last year.
"Unless there is a big snowstorm two days before Christmas, people are going to buy. It's the gift-giving season," he said.
Sears, Roebuck and Co., for example, said last weekend's sales were solidly "on plan."

"The average consumer is time-stressed and looking for a place to meet all of his or her shopping needs quickly," John Costello, Sears senior executive vice president of marketing, said in an interview Sunday.
"Plus, this is great shopping weather -- not too cold and no major snowstorms," Costello said.

TeleCheck, which monitors sales paid by check nationwide, said Tuesday its data showed a 5 percent gain over last year for sales in stores open more than a year during the first 17 days of this shopping season. Checks account for more than one-third of retail spending, according to Telecheck.
The International Council of Shopping Centers said it expected holiday sales in the nation's regional malls to be up "in the mid-single digits".
Clothing and jewelry are a top choice for gifts this season, but consumer electronics and personal computers, which lack a blockbuster product like last year's Windows 95 software, are lagging.

The economy is generally healthy and consumer confidence is strong, and this has helped boost sales of more expensive items in the hot apparel sector, such as cashmere sweaters and winter coats, analysts said.
This year's vibrant colors, such as lime and robin's egg blue, have added an extra dose of temptation.

"I think fashion right now is benefiting the retailers," said Michael Conn, an analyst for brokerage Gruntal & Co. Inc. "There are a lot of bright colors, not just your basic browns and blacks, and that bodes well for the retailers."

Saul Yaari, brokerage Piper Jaffray Inc.'s retail analyst, said he expected a 5 percent increase in overall holiday sales compared with last year, thanks largely to strong clothing, jewelry and footwear sales, but "any one day that forces people to stay in their homes would be detrimental".
"Every day counts and every day is important. And, hopefully, there won't be any snowstorms, so consumers will continue to shop aggressively," said Yaari.
